items.canonical_answer: Residents should agree which activities are offered, access limits, consent and how local guides or suppliers retain earnings. This links feasible income to community control rather than assuming access to private practices.
marking_guidance: Context: income aim and stated cultural concern.
Reason: match consent and retained benefits.

items.prompt: Explain whether cultural tourism fits a fictional community with willing paid guides but disagreement over showing private ceremonies. A guided public-history walk is an alternative.

marking_guidance: Judgement: weigh income and consent.

items.prompt: Explain whether a fictional conservation visitor scheme suits local well-being when habitats are protected but grazing access is restricted and residents receive no work or supply contracts.
items.canonical_answer: Habitat protection is a benefit, but livelihood costs and absent local income links weaken the proposal. Participation and workable benefit/access arrangements are needed; a conservation label alone does not resolve the trade-off.
marking_guidance: Judgement: conditional suitability for local well-being.
Reason: weigh protection with access costs and retained-benefit gaps.

items.prompt: Explain the income mechanism where a fictional visitor centre buys local produce and hires local guides, while confirmed visitors can reach it.
items.canonical_answer: Visitor demand creates paid work and sales for participating households, retaining some spending locally. The access and local supply/employment links make the gain plausible; visitor numbers alone would not establish it.
marking_guidance: Mechanism: visitor spending through local work and purchases.
Consequence: retained household income under supplied demand/access.

items.prompt: State (a) one production obstacle and one marketing obstacle [2]. Explain (b) why a seed loan may fail to improve an invented group’s sales when it already has stored crops and buyers but the market road is blocked [4].
items.canonical_answer: (a) Insufficient growing water; a blocked route to buyers. (b) The constraint lies in selling existing output, not producing more. Seed credit adds debt and potential crops without restoring delivery; a feasible access response addresses the stated mechanism.
marking_guidance: Point: two correctly distinguished obstacles [2].
Development: use both existing output/buyers and blocked access, then explain why the loan misses the constraint [4].

items.prompt: Describe (a) this fictional comparison for 100 harvested bags: A loses 30 before sale; B loses 10, with the same available buyers [3]. Suggest (b) a priority if the aim is higher useful sales without more land clearance, and a feasible storage repair is available for A [3].
items.canonical_answer: (a) B has 90 usable bags versus A’s 70, so lower storage loss accompanies 20 more useful bags from the same harvest. (b) Repair A’s storage and maintain it: reducing avoidable loss can improve sales without expanding cleared land. Buyers and repair feasibility make this a matched response.
marking_guidance: Evidence: compare loss and useful output [3].
Meaning: justify the storage priority against useful sales and unchanged land use [3].
